correspondences.rationale: Both denote an optical EDFA amplifier unit used in the line.
Both denote the booster-amplifier role at the transmitting/head end of an OMS.
Both denote the inline amplifier role at an intermediate line-amplifier site.
Both denote the preamplifier role at the receiving/tail end of an OMS.
Both denote an OTN switch providing ODU cross-connect functionality.
Both denote a client-facing port; the VA concept is explicitly the resource role that raises client-port alarms.
Both denote a ROADM device. The VA concept further specifies a colourless, directionless and contentionless implementation.
OPR-15 denotes received optical power reported in 15-minute performance-monitoring bins.
ES-15 denotes line errored seconds in 15-minute performance-monitoring bins.
The vendor monitor OSNR-EST is estimated OSNR, matching receiver-DSP-estimated OSNR rather than OCM OSNR.
Both denote pre-FEC bit error ratio at the coherent receiver.
Both denote differential group delay.
Both denote the rate of change of the state of polarisation.
Both denote transmitter laser bias current as a percentage of beginning-of-life current.
Composite input power is the total optical power measured at an amplifier input.
Composite output power is the total optical power measured at an amplifier output.
Both denote amplifier pump drive current as a percentage of beginning-of-life current.
Both denote a monitor, exemplified by an OSC receiver, used only to generate alarms and not to report values.
Client ES denotes client errored seconds; the shared-vocabulary concept makes the implied 15-minute PM interval explicit.
Client UAS denotes client unavailable seconds; the shared-vocabulary concept makes the implied 15-minute PM interval explicit.
Both denote per-channel optical power reported by a ROADM optical channel monitor.
VA's Standard availability condition corresponds to the shared baseline monitoring package; OPR-15 is a standard 15-minute performance counter.
Both denote availability under the optical power-monitoring option, with OPR being an optical power monitor.
OSNR-EST is an advanced coherent-DSP-derived telemetry quantity, aligning with the shared coherent advanced-telemetry category.
Both explicitly denote optical channel monitoring availability under an OCM option or licence.
Both denote absence of detectable optical signal at the receiver.
Both denote a channel or signal having reduced optical power.
An OSC not being received is the span-local loss of the optical supervisory channel.
Both denote reduced optical signal-to-noise ratio.
Both denote a rapid state-of-polarisation change.
The vendor card-failure condition causes loss of traffic and silent monitoring, matching the shared unit-down condition.
Both denote loss of OTU frame alignment.
Both denote pre-FEC errors above the OTU degrade threshold while framing remains available.
Both denote an ODU alarm indication signal propagating on the ODU path.
Both denote an ODU sent to the wrong destination by a cross-connect.
Both denote interruption of the client service.
Both denote a brief client-service interruption associated with protection switching.
The shared pump-ageing condition is defined by pump drive current rising to maintain gain.
Both denote rising transmit-laser bias current as the laser ages.
Both denote a slow decline in channel margin.
Both concepts describe independent per-channel switching, where an ingress line-wide impairment persists on each channel routed to an egress degree.
Both denote hard failure or shutdown of a transponder transmit laser, causing loss of light at the receiver.
Both denote a hard equipment-card failure; A additionally describes resulting traffic and alarm effects.
Both denote degradation localized to a coherent receiver, producing errors or receiver penalty while the optical path remains normal.
A's rising laser bias current preceding failure is the ageing-related upward bias-current drift described by B.
Both denote a slow decline in optical-channel margin.
Both denote a severed fibre that prevents light from passing.
B explicitly covers either pump-laser or whole-amplifier failure resulting in no amplifier output, matching a dead EDFA.
A pulled jumper is a disconnected connector or patch cord as defined by B.
Both denote abnormally increased attenuation on an upstream fibre span.
Both denote an increase in differential group delay on the fibre path.
Both denote a WSS channel passband shifted from its intended centre frequency.
Both denote a rapid transient change in fibre state of polarisation.
Both denote connector contamination that adds optical loss.
Both are catch-all causes for an unspecified failure on the path toward the far end.
Both denote amplifier gain falling below its target or set point.
Both denote an amplifier becoming noisier through an increased noise figure.
Both denote ageing of an amplifier pump manifested by upward drift of pump drive current.
Both denote amplifier gain ceasing to be flat across the optical band.
Both denote failure of an OTN switching fabric, interrupting ODUs traversing it.
Both denote an incorrectly configured OTN cross-connect delivering an ODU to the wrong destination.
Both denote failure of a client port or its associated optical module.
Both denote drift in a WSS channel's attenuation setting, changing that channel's output power.
Both denote hard failure of a WSS port; A specifies an ingress port and its effect on all channels entering through it.
Both denote a hard fault causing loss of service; transmit laser failure produces loss of signal and thus an outage.
Both denote degradation rather than total failure, with traffic or reception continuing at reduced quality.
Both denote a developing trend, such as laser ageing, that precedes failure before traffic is affected.
Both denote every optical channel in the multiplexed signal.
Both denote one optical channel; the A concept explicitly scopes the symptom to one channel.
Channels at one band edge are a subset of the multiplexed channels, matching B's explicit example of some, but not all, channels.
B defines port as every channel arriving on one ROADM degree's input port, exactly matching A's traffic scope. A's similarly named client port denotes a physical endpoint and is a false cognate.
The card itself is the affected unit, as opposed to traffic carried by it.
Both explicitly denote this receiver only.
A specifies all ODUs through the switch, which is exactly B's every ODU cross-connected through the switch.
Both denote one ODU.
Both denote the affected client service.
“Locally” denotes the faulty/local unit where the change is observed, corresponding to the unit that raised the alarm or saw the change.
Both denote the specific port raising the equipment or port alarm.
The incoming span is the fibre span immediately upstream of the unit.
The previous EDFA is the immediately upstream optical amplifier.
Both denote the input connection of the optical multiplex section.
Both denote any applicable location before the unit along the channel's signal path.
Both denote the remote line transmitter supplying light to the local receiver.
Both denote the remote line interface receiving the channel transmitted by the local unit.
Both denote the signal path between the unit and the far-end line interface in the far-end direction.
In context, both denote a client service port at either endpoint.
Both denote an OTN switch or cross-connect on the service's ODU path.
Both denote the working ODU path and the elements on which it depends.
Both denote the protection ODU path and the elements on which it depends.
Both denote the ODU path currently carrying the service.
Both denote the critical alarm severity.
Both denote the minor alarm severity.
Both denote a reported condition that is not alarmed.
Both denote the major alarm severity.
